856: On the night of the 17th day of the 10th month, the assassin Yoritomo had sent, *Tosa-bō Shōshun*, fell upon Yoshitsune's mansion at Rokujō-Horikawa with some sixty horsemen. Yoshitsune had only a handful of retainers about him; he armed himself and went out to meet them, and it was *Shizuka Gozen* who helped him into his armour. Shōshun was routed, taken, and beheaded.
857: “Lord Kurō, your armour is here.” Shizuka Gozen tied the cords of his dōmaru.
858: The next day, Yoshitsune and his uncle Yukiie knelt in your courtyard.
859: “My brother means to kill me. I ask for no rank and no reward — only a single In-zen from the Cloistered Emperor, so that I need not die like a common thief.”
860: You know that to set this In-zen to paper is to stake everything on one throw.
861: The Koshigoe Letter appears in the Azuma Kagami under the 24th day of the 5th month of Bunji 1; its authenticity is disputed.
862: The night attack at Horikawa is recorded in the Azuma Kagami and the Gyokuyō. Go-Shirakawa issued a senji ordering the subjugation of Yoritomo on the 18th day of the 10th month.
863: Issue an In-zen to subjugate Yoritomo
864: Refuse, and send Yoshitsune on his way
866: Issue the In-zen, and back Yoshitsune with the Northern Guard, the warrior-monks of the Mountain, and the levies of the home provinces
867: Give him not just a sheet of paper, but an army
870: The warriors of the home provinces did not answer Yoshitsune's call. On the 3rd day of the 11th month, Yoshitsune and Yukiie left the capital and went west, meaning to reach Kyūshū; at Daimotsu-ura in Settsu a storm overturned their ships, and the party was scattered. Shizuka Gozen was captured in the mountains of Yoshino.
871: On the 11th day of the 11th month, you issued another In-zen: Yoshitsune and Yukiie were to be hunted down.
872: Yoritomo's answer was to send his father-in-law, *Hōjō Tokimasa*, into the capital with a thousand horse. With him came a letter, addressed to your favourite Takashina no Yasutsune, yet plainly meant for your eyes:
873: “That the rebellion of Yukiie and Yoshitsune was the work of the heavenly demons — this is a strange thing to say. Heavenly demons are those who obstruct the Buddha's Law and trouble the bonds of men… And who is the Greatest Tengu in Japan, if not someone else entirely?”
874: “Your Majesty,” Yasutsune's hands were trembling, “th-this was written to me…”
876: You read it once by lamplight, and then again.
877: At the foot of the letter was a single line in small characters, in Yoritomo's own hand: “Twenty years in Izu, and the sutra scroll always at my side.” You went still.
878: “The Lord of Kamakura's wish is this: to place *shugo* in every province and *jitō* on the estates, and to levy commissariat rice at five shō per tan. He begs the Cloistered Emperor's sanction.”
879: The “Great Tengu” letter is recorded in the Gyokuyō under the 26th day of the 11th month of Bunji 1, and in the Azuma Kagami under the 15th day of the 11th month of Bunji 1.
880: The sanction of shugo and jitō (the Bunji Sanction) was granted on the 28th day of the 11th month of Bunji 1, and was the keystone of the Kamakura shogunate's order.
881: Lay the blame on Yasutsune and sanction the shugo and jitō
882: Answer with an imayō: tengu can sing, too
883: A mocking imayō, sent off to Kamakura
885: Refuse the request for shugo and jitō
886: Requires Authority enough to face down Tokimasa's thousand horse
889: You summoned Kujō Kanezane and Yoshida Tsunefusa, and sent envoys to Enryaku-ji, Kōfuku-ji and the other great houses, to tell them: once the jitō are in place, the rents of every estate will pass into the hands of the eastern warriors.
890: For the first time, the nobles and the temples stood on the same side as you. Tokimasa lingered in the capital three months, and seeing the court in uproar, he gave ground: the jitō would be placed only on lands confiscated from the Taira and from rebels, not on every estate in the realm.
891: When Yoritomo heard, he said only: “The Cloistered Emperor is the Cloistered Emperor, after all.”
892: This is a partially rewritten line. Historically, the shugo and jitō were somewhat curtailed the following year, but the principle was still sanctioned.
894: A Thousand Horse at the Gate
895: You refused. Tokimasa did not argue; he merely let his thousand horse stay on in the capital a while longer.
896: Every dawn, the hoofbeats of eastern warriors rang outside Hōjūji-dono. The nobles dared not come to court; the temples kept their gates shut.
897: On the seventh day, you summoned Tokimasa and set your kaō upon the letter of sanction.
901: In the 3rd month of Bunji 2, Yoritomo put forward *Kujō Kanezane* as Regent. Kanezane had been your critic for years; his diary is full of complaints against you. Now he would sit beside you at court.
902: On the 8th day of the 4th month, at Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū in Kamakura, the captive Shizuka Gozen was made to dance before Yoritomo and his wife. Yet what she sang was her longing for Yoshitsune:
903: 「しづやしづ　しづのをだまき　くり返し　昔を今に　なすよしもがな」
904: “Calm yourself, my lord. When you were in Izu, I longed for you day and night just so.” Yoritomo was in a fury; so Hōjō Masako counselled him.
905: That same spring, you slipped quietly out of the capital and went to Jakkō-in in Ōhara to see Kenreimon-in.
906: The mountain path was wild and lonely, the summer grass deep. Her hermitage was a poor thing; she was up on the hill gathering flowers, and when she saw you she could not speak for shock. She was your adopted daughter, the mother of your grandson.
907: “Your Majesty… to come to such mountains as these…”
908: Kneeling before you, she slowly told of all she had passed through in her life — heaven, the human world, the asuras, the hungry ghosts, the beasts, and hell: the *Six Realms*.
909: “…The Nun of the Second Rank took the late Emperor in her arms and said there was a capital beneath the sea too. I leapt as well. But they caught my hair with rakes. Your Majesty — why was it me they left behind?”
910: As you left, you looked back and saw her standing before the hermitage, watching you go until you were out of sight.
911: The Imperial Visit to Ōhara (Bunji 2) appears in the “Initiates' Chapter” of The Tale of the Heike, which closes the whole work.
912: Shizuka Gozen's dance at Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is recorded in the Azuma Kagami under the 8th day of the 4th month of Bunji 2.
913: Listen quietly to her tale of the Six Realms
914: This is a debt you have carried all your life
915: On returning, charge Kanezane with setting the court in order
916: The Regents' house may yet rise again
917: On returning, confer with Lady Tango over the Chōkōdō estates
918: Your daughter Senyōmon-in will inherit the greatest cluster of estates in the realm
922: In the 2nd month of Bunji 3, Yoshitsune, disguised as a mountain ascetic, fled with his wife and child, Benkei and the rest along the Hokurikudō to Hiraizumi in Mutsu, to seek the protector of his boyhood, the third lord of the Ōshū Fujiwara, *Fujiwara no Hidehira*.
923: The Golden Hall of Hiraizumi glittered in the snow. Hidehira commanded a hundred and seventy thousand horse — the only power that could stand against Kamakura.
924: Again and again Yoritomo petitioned: send a senji to Ōshū, ordering them to hand over Yoshitsune.
925: In the autumn of Bunji 3, word came from Hiraizumi: Hidehira was ill. He was past sixty; of his sons, the eldest, Kunihira, was born of a concubine, and the heir, *Yasuhira*, was timid. Once Hidehira died, no one could say which way Ōshū would lean.
926: “Your Majesty,” Lady Tango said softly at your side, “Hiraizumi has sent a good deal of gold these past years.”
927: Hidehira died on the 29th day of the 10th month of Bunji 3; his dying instructions are recorded in the Gyokuyō.
928: The battle of Koromogawa took place on the 30th day of the intercalary 4th month of Bunji 5; Benkei's “standing death” is a legend recorded in the Gikeiki.
929: At Yoritomo's request, send a senji to Ōshū
930: While Hidehira still lives, send a secret In-zen to Hiraizumi
931: Have Ōshū raise Yoshitsune up and hold out against Kamakura
936: On the 29th day of the 10th month, Hidehira died of his illness. Before the end he gathered his sons and left his last command: make Yoshitsune your general, and resist Kamakura.
937: But Yasuhira feared Yoritomo, and feared your senji still more. On the 30th day of the intercalary 4th month of Bunji 5, he led several hundred horse against the Koromogawa residence. Benkei stood before the gate, pierced by countless arrows, still upright on his halberd, and did not fall even in death — what the world calls the *standing death*. Yoshitsune killed his wife and daughter, then himself. He was thirty-one. His head was steeped in fine sake, sealed in a black-lacquered chest, and sent to Koshigoe outside Kamakura.
938: Yoshitsune was dead, yet Yoritomo did not stand down his army. He petitioned for the subjugation of Yasuhira.
939: You hesitated — Yasuhira had obeyed the senji and struck down Yoshitsune; what was his crime? The senji was slow in coming. On the 19th day of the 7th month, Yoritomo, not waiting for it, rode out of Kamakura at the head of two hundred and eighty thousand horse and marched north by three roads.
940: In the 8th month, at the battle of Atsukashi-yama, the army of Ōshū broke. Yasuhira abandoned Hiraizumi and fled, putting to the torch every hall but the Golden Hall. On the 3rd day of the 9th month, Yasuhira was slain by his own retainer. Four generations and a hundred years of the Ōshū Fujiwara ended there.
941: After the fact, you issued the senji of subjugation, and dated it the 19th day of the 7th month.
942: From that day, there was no army left in all Japan that could defy Kamakura.
943: The Ōshū Campaign is recorded in the Azuma Kagami. When Yoritomo marched, no senji had yet been issued; it was issued afterward and backdated to the day he set out.
947: In the 11th month of Kenkyū 1, Yoritomo came up to the capital with more than a thousand horse. It was the first time he had returned to Kyoto since the Heiji Disturbance — he had been thirteen then; now he was forty-four.
948: You received him at Rokujō-dono. The two of you sat face to face, attendants dismissed, and talked the whole day through. Over the following month and more, you met in secret eight times in all. What was said, no one knows.
949: You granted him the posts of Acting Major Counsellor and Major Captain of the Right Palace Guards. He resigned them, keeping only the title of “former Major Captain of the Right”. It was not rank in the capital that he wanted.
950: He was a little shorter than you had imagined, broad of face, slow of speech, every word seemingly weighed on a scale.
951: From the fold of his robe he drew out a sutra scroll, its paper gone yellow: “This was granted me by Your Majesty in the second year of Heiji.”
952: “In the second year of Heiji, Your Majesty argued that I should be beheaded,” he said suddenly. “I have always remembered.”
953: “In the year of Heiji I was only thirteen. I once glimpsed Your Majesty's carriage from afar.”
954: “You wrote that We are the Great Tengu.”
956: “No, you were right. But do you know why the tengu lives in the mountains? — Because there is no place for it below.”
957: You looked at him and thought of Yoshitomo, Yoshinaka, Yoshitsune — the men of the Minamoto, who one after another walked into your palace and one after another died. Only the man before you had never once let you grip the hilt of his sword.
958: Yoritomo's visit to the capital and his talks with Go-Shirakawa are recorded in the Gyokuyō and the Azuma Kagami, in entries from the 11th to the 12th month of Kenkyū 1.
962: Cross words with him and sound his depths
964: Deal with him openly and entrust him with the realm
965: Perhaps he was the one who was right
969: In the spring of Kenkyū 3, you fell ill.
970: In Rokujō-dono, Lady Tango kept watch at your bedside, and Senyōmon-in held your hand. Beyond the window lay the roof of the Chōkōdō, and farther off, the Eastern Hills.
971: You remembered many things. The autumn rain at Sanjō-Takakura, Otomae's hoarse singing, the fire at Shirakawa-kita-dono, the court ladies in the well at Sanjō-dono, the moonlight on the sea at Itsukushima, Kenshunmon-in's face in profile, the fence at Toba-dono, the fire at Hōjūji-dono, the eyes of the Great Buddha, the tide at Dan-no-ura.
972: You saw five emperors to their end: Nijō, Rokujō, Takakura, Antoku — and yourself. You saw off Shinzei, Nobuyori, Kiyomori, Shigemori, Yoshitomo, Yoshinaka, Yoshitsune. You outlived them all.
973: On the 13th day of the 3rd month, at the hour of the Tiger, you turned to the west, the nenbutsu on your lips, and passed away in peace. You were sixty-six.
974: “Your Majesty, what else would you like to hear?”
976: Those who came after said you were the Greatest Tengu in Japan. Yet the last song you sang was one you had learned as a boy.
980: The fires of Rokuhara died out. Munemori knelt in the courtyard of Hōjūji-dono and begged pardon on his father's behalf. Kiyomori lay ill at Fukuhara, and the young men of his house were in turmoil.
981: For the first time since Hōgen, it was not warriors striking down warriors in the Emperor's name — it was the In-zen itself that had defeated the strongest warrior house in the realm.
982: The capital buzzed with talk. The warrior-monks of Enryaku-ji paraded along the Shijō riverbank, proclaiming it the divine power of Hiyoshi Sannō. The exile Yoritomo in Izu and Yoshinaka in Kiso both watched and waited.
983: Your favourites waited eagerly for your command: destroy the Taira!
984: But you were thinking of something else: if the Taira were gone, who would be the next to take up the sword?
985: This is an imagined line: if the In's forces had defeated the Taira, what form would cloistered rule have taken?
986: Summon Yoritomo of Izu and Yoshinaka of Kiso, and wipe out the Taira
988: Let the Taira withdraw to hold the western provinces, as a bulwark of the royal house
989: Keep one tiger to guard against another
990: Lean on neither Minamoto nor Taira; stand alone with the Northern Guard and the temples' troops
991: The Throne's army, led by the Throne
995: The Taira fled west, pursued onto the sea by the Minamoto. But between Yoritomo and Yoshinaka, a rift soon opened.
996: Yoshinaka held the capital, Yoritomo the east. Both called themselves your servants; both begged you for an In-zen to strike down the other.
997: You understood a truth: a single sword will sooner or later turn on its wielder; with two, you can set them hacking at each other.
998: Use In-zen to keep the two Minamoto in check, and never let one house stand supreme
999: Requires the heart of a tengu
1001: Rely on Yoritomo as the realm's great general
1002: Kamakura's order may be better than no order at all
1003: While the two Minamoto quarrel, raise up the Emperor's personal rule
1007: Guardian of the West, Warden of the East
1008: The Taira withdrew to Fukuhara and the western provinces, and Munemori was named Great General Pacifier of the West. In the east Yoritomo rose in arms, but you issued an In-zen commanding Taira and Minamoto each to hold their own ground and not cross the line.
1009: Both houses hated you, yet neither could do without you: without the In-zen, the Taira were “enemies of the court” and Yoritomo merely “an exile”.
1010: The realm was like a balance, and you were its fulcrum.
1013: After the forty-ninth-day rites for Kenshunmon-in, you summoned Kiyomori to Hōjūji-dono, dismissed your attendants, and the two of you drank together deep into the night.
1014: “While she lived, there was no need for many words between us. Now that she is gone — I am afraid.”
1015: “So am I,” you said. “That is why we must speak plainly.”
1016: You made a pact: the In's domains would not encroach on the Taira's proprietary provinces, and the Taira would not meddle in appointments within the In's household. Shigemori would act as go-between, with Tokitada as his second, and they would meet each month.
1017: The men of Shishigatani — Narichika, Saikō, Shunkan — were still meeting in secret. They came to invite you to a banquet to view the moon.
1019: Politely decline the banquet, and quietly warn Narichika to stop
1020: Protect your favourites, and the pact as well
1021: Tell Shigemori of the Shishigatani affair and have him deal leniently
1022: Their lives, entrusted to Shigemori's benevolence
1025: Shigemori died. Keeping to the pact, you let Koremori retain Echizen. Kiyomori sent Munemori to thank you.
1026: In Jishō 4, your son Prince Mochihito plotted a rising with Minamoto no Yorimasa and sent a prince's edict to the Minamoto in every province. When the plot came to light, Prince Mochihito fled to Nara.
1028: You looked him in the eye: “I did not.” — And it was the truth.
1029: The fire in the east had already been lit. Yoritomo in Izu and Yoshinaka in Kiso had both received the edict. Kiyomori had grown old, and his cough worsened by the day.
1030: Join Kiyomori in decreeing war on the east, but spare Prince Mochihito's life
1032: Urge Kiyomori toward conciliation with the east
1033: To subdue the enemy without fighting
1037: Kiyomori was gravely ill. You went in person to the Nishihachijō mansion to see him — the Cloistered Emperor himself at the sickbed of the lay-priest Chancellor of the Realm, a thing never seen before.
1038: He seized your hand: “Munemori… is not the man Shigemori was. Your Majesty — the Taira, I leave them in your keeping.”
1039: He died. For the first time, cloistered rule and the Taira became true allies.
1040: In the 8th month, a secret memorial from Yoritomo arrived as well: divide the realm east and west, with Minamoto and Taira side by side.
1041: Grant the division of east and west, with the In at the centre
1043: Rally the realm by In-zen and march on the east with the Taira
1044: Requires strong Taira and sufficient Authority
1047: Three times you summoned Munemori. The third time, you said nothing of Yoritomo; you spoke only of his mother Tokiko, of Kenshunmon-in, of that night on the sea at Itsukushima.
1048: “My late father's last words…” Munemori wept.
1049: “The Lay Priest Chancellor's last wish was for the Taira to endure,” you said, “not for the Taira to perish.”
1050: At last Munemori nodded. The In-zen was issued: the provinces of the Tōkaidō and Tōsandō were entrusted to Yoritomo's governance; the circuits of the west to the Taira; and the appointment and dismissal of provincial governors would issue from the In alone.
1051: Yoshinaka would not submit and took up arms alone in the Hokuriku, and Yoritomo and the Taira put him down together. The realm settled into peace, the warriors of the two houses staring at one another across Hakone and Suzuka.
1052: This is an imagined line. Historically, Munemori rejected Yoritomo's proposal to divide the realm.
1055: The In of the Western Sea
1056: You left the capital with the Taira fleet. As the ships passed Suma, you looked back to see the sky over the capital glowing red with the great fire of Rokuhara.
1057: Your presence lifted the spirits of the whole Taira house. Munemori knelt at the prow: “With the Cloistered Emperor among us, we are no enemies of the court.”
1058: At Dazaifu, you issued an In-zen: should a new emperor be raised in the capital, he would be a false emperor; Yoshinaka and Yoritomo alike were enemies of the court.
1059: In the capital, the nobles were at a loss — with no decree from the Cloistered Emperor and no sacred regalia, whomever they enthroned would lack all legitimacy. In the end, the Regent Motomichi and the others could only raise the fourth prince, Takahira, by “deliberation of the lords”.
1060: Two courts, two emperors — one on the sea, one in the capital.
1061: This is an imagined line. Historically, Go-Shirakawa slipped away to Mount Hiei and did not go west with the Taira.
1062: Muster the army at Yashima, resolved to retake the capital
1063: In the name of the In-zen and the sacred regalia
1064: Hold the western provinces and face down the capital
1065: Trade time for the hearts of men
1067: The great Taira host marched east from Yashima and drew up at Ichi-no-Tani, west of the old capital of Fukuhara. You held court at Fukuhara, and your In-zen were posted at every village gate in Settsu and Harima: all who came over would be pardoned their past offences and confirmed in their lands.
1068: The eastern army came. Noriyori struck at the Ikuta Wood from the front, while Yoshitsune led seventy horsemen round to the heights of Hiyodorigoe.
1069: But this time, Taira no Noritsune had long since laid an ambush at the foot of the Hiyodorigoe cliffs. As Yoshitsune's riders came plunging down, arrows rained from the woods on either side.
1070: No one had imagined that anyone would ride down a cliff like that.
1074: You did not let Yoshitsune leave the capital alone. The Northern Guard and the Western Guard, the warrior-monks of Enryaku-ji and Onjō-ji, the warriors of the estates of the home provinces — all gathered at Rokujō-Horikawa under your In-zen.
1075: Hōjō Tokimasa's thousand horse reached Ōmi, saw the banners standing like a forest in the capital, and halted.
1076: Yoshitsune was the finest field commander in the realm. What he had always lacked was never courage, but legitimacy and support. Now you had given him both.
1077: “If the Lord of Kamakura comes,” Benkei laughed, drinking in the courtyard, “I'll be waiting for him on the Gojō Bridge!”
1078: But Kamakura's two hundred thousand horse would come in the end. You needed a greater alliance.
1079: This is an imagined line. Historically, the warriors of the home provinces did not answer Yoshitsune's summons, and he was forced to leave the capital.
